nodes.name: Saias-Weingartner theorem
nodes.statement:
In \cite{SW}, Saias and Weingartner showed that if
$L(s)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty\frac{\lambda(m)}{m^s}$ is a Dirichlet series
with periodic coefficients, then either $L(s)=0$ for some $s$ with real
part $>1$, or $\lambda(m)$ is multiplicative at almost all primes (so
that $L(s)=D(s)L(s,\chi)$ for some primitive Dirichlet character $\chi$
and finite Dirichlet series $D$).
nodes.statement_short: A Dirichlet series with periodic coefficients either vanishes somewhere in $\Re(s)>1$ or is essentially $D(s)L(s,\chi)$.
assumptions: $L(s)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty\frac{\lambda(m)}{m^s}$ is a Dirichlet series with periodic coefficients
conclusions: either $L(s)=0$ for some $s$ with real part $>1$, or $\lambda(m)$ is multiplicative at almost all primes (so that $L(s)=D(s)L(s,\chi)$ for some primitive Dirichlet character $\chi$ and finite Dirichlet series $D$)

nodes.name: Davenport-Heilbronn theorem on Hurwitz and Epstein zeta-functions
nodes.statement:
Earlier work of Davenport and Heilbronn
\cite{dh1,dh2} established this result for the special case of the Hurwitz
zeta-function $\zeta(s,\alpha)$ with rational parameter $\alpha$, and
proved an analogue for the degree $2$ Epstein zeta-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Hurwitz zeta-functions with rational parameter (and analogously Epstein zeta-functions) have zeros in the half-plane of absolute convergence.
assumptions: the Hurwitz zeta-function $\zeta(s,\alpha)$ with rational parameter $\alpha$
conclusions: established this result for the special case of the Hurwitz zeta-function $\zeta(s,\alpha)$ with rational parameter $\alpha$, and proved an analogue for the degree $2$ Epstein zeta-functions

nodes.name: Conrey-Ghosh theorem
nodes.statement:
Also in
degree $2$, Conrey and Ghosh \cite{cg} showed that the $L$-function
associated to the square of Ramanujan's $\Delta$ modular form has
infinitely many zeros outside of its critical strip.
assumptions: the $L$-function associated to the square of Ramanujan's $\Delta$ modular form
conclusions: has infinitely many zeros outside of its critical strip

nodes.name: Theorem 1.1 (classical holomorphic cuspforms)
nodes.statement:
Let $f\in S_k(\Gamma_1(N))$ be a holomorphic cuspform of arbitrary
weight and level. If the associated complete $L$-function
$\Lambda_f(s)=\int_0^\infty f(iy)y^{s-1}\,dy$ does not vanish for
$\Re(s)>\frac{k+1}2$ then $f$ is an eigenfunction of the Hecke operators
$T_p$ for all primes $p\nmid N$.
nodes.statement_short: A holomorphic cuspform whose complete $L$-function has no zeros in $\Re(s)>\frac{k+1}2$ is a Hecke eigenform.
assumptions: Let $f\in S_k(\Gamma_1(N))$ be a holomorphic cuspform of arbitrary weight and level.
the associated complete $L$-function $\Lambda_f(s)=\int_0^\infty f(iy)y^{s-1}\,dy$ does not vanish for $\Re(s)>\frac{k+1}2$
conclusions: $f$ is an eigenfunction of the Hecke operators $T_p$ for all primes $p\nmid N$
nodes.label: thm:classical

nodes.name: Theorem 1.2 (main theorem)
nodes.statement:
Fix a positive integer $n$. For $j=1,\ldots,n$, let $r_j$ be
a positive integer and $\pi_j$ a unitary cuspidal automorphic
representation of $\mathrm{GL}_{r_j}(\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ with $L$-series
$L(s,\pi_j)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty\lambda_j(m)m^{-s}$.  Assume that the
$\pi_j$ satisfy the generalized Ramanujan conjecture at all finite places
(so that, in particular, $|\lambda_j(p)|\le r_j$ for all primes $p$)
and are pairwise non-isomorphic. Let
$$
R=\left\{\sum_{m=1}^M\frac{a_m}{m^s}:M\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0},
(a_1,\ldots,a_M)\in\mathbb{C}^M\right\}
$$
denote the ring of finite Dirichlet series, and let $P\in
R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ be a polynomial with coefficients in $R$.
Then either $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ has a zero with real
part $>1$ or $P=D(s)x_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ for some $D\in R$,
$d_1,\ldots,d_n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$.
nodes.statement_short: A polynomial in pairwise non-isomorphic automorphic $L$-functions (Ramanujan assumed) with finite Dirichlet series coefficients vanishes somewhere in $\Re(s)>1$ unless it is a monomial.
assumptions: Fix a positive integer $n$.

For $j=1,\ldots,n$, let $r_j$ be a positive integer and $\pi_j$ a unitary cuspidal automorphic representation of $\mathrm{GL}_{r_j}(\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ with $L$-series $L(s,\pi_j)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty\lambda_j(m)m^{-s}$.
Assume that the $\pi_j$ satisfy the generalized Ramanujan conjecture at all finite places (so that, in particular, $|\lambda_j(p)|\le r_j$ for all primes $p$) and are pairwise non-isomorphic.
let $P\in R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ be a polynomial with coefficients in $R$.
conclusions: Then either $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ has a zero with real part $>1$ or $P=D(s)x_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ for some $D\in R$, $d_1,\ldots,d_n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$.
nodes.label: thm:main

nodes.name: Remarks on Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement:
\hspace{1cm}
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $\pi_j$ as in the statement of the theorem, it is known
(see \cite{jacquet-shalika}) that $L(s,\pi_j)$ does not vanish for
$\Re(s)\ge1$. Thus if $P=D(s)x_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ is a monomial
then whether or not $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ vanishes
for some $s$ with $\Re(s)>1$ is determined entirely by the finite
Dirichlet series $D(s)$.  Further, the Grand Riemann Hypothesis (GRH)
predicts that each $L(s,\pi_j)$ does not vanish for $\Re(s)>\frac12$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} demonstrates that the GRH, if it is true,
is a very rigid phenomenon.

\item By the almost-periodicity of Dirichlet series, if
$P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ has at least one zero with real part $>1$
then it must have infinitely many such zeros. In fact, our proof shows
that there is some number $\eta=\eta(P;\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n)>0$ such that
for any $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ with $1<\sigma_1<\sigma_2\le1+\eta$, we have
\begin{equation} \#\bigl\{s\in\mathbb{C}:\Re(s)\in[\sigma_1,\sigma_2], \Im(s)\in[-T,T],
P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))=0\bigr\}
\gg T
\end{equation}
for $T$ sufficiently large (where both the implied constant and the
meaning of ``sufficiently large'' depend on $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$
as well as $P$ and $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n$).

On the other hand, if we restrict to $\mathbb{C}$-linear combinations
(i.e.\ homogeneous degree $1$ polynomials $P\in\mathbb{C}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$)
and $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n$ with a common conductor and archimedean
component $\pi_{1,\infty}\cong\ldots\cong\pi_{n,\infty}$, Bombieri and
Hejhal \cite{bh} showed, subject to GRH and a weak form of the pair
correlation conjecture for $L(s,\pi_j)$, that asymptotically $100\%$
of the non-trivial zeros of $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ have real
part $\frac12$.

\item The assumption of the Ramanujan conjecture in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}
could be relaxed. For instance, it would suffice to have, for each
fixed $j$:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)]some mild control over the
coefficients of the logarithmic derivative
$$\frac{L'}{L}(s,\pi_j)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty c_j(m)m^{-s}$$
at prime powers, namely
$\sum_p\frac{|c_j(p^k)|^2}{p^k}<\infty$
for any fixed $k\ge2$ (cf.\ \cite[Hypothesis H]{rs});
\item[(ii)]an average bound for $|\lambda_j(p)|^4$ over arithmetic
progressions of primes, namely
$$
\limsup_{x\to\infty}
\frac{\sum_{\substack{p\le x\\p\equiv a\;(\text{mod }q)}}|\lambda_j(p)|^4}
{\sum_{\substack{p\le x\\p\equiv a\;(\text{mod }q)}}1}
\le C_j,
$$
for all co-prime $a,q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, where $C_j>0$ is independent of $a,q$.
\end{itemize}
Note that (i) is known to hold when $r_j\le 4$ (see \cite{rs,kim}).
Further, both estimates follow from the Rankin--Selberg method if,
for instance, the tensor square $\pi_j\otimes\pi_j$ is automorphic
for each $j$. Since this is known when $r_j=2$ (see \cite{gj}),
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} could be extended to include the $L$-functions
associated to Maass forms.

\item The main tool used in the proof is the quasi-orthogonality of
the coefficients $\lambda_j(p)$, i.e.\ asymptotic estimates for sums of
the form $\sum_{p\le x}\frac{\lambda_j(p)\overline{\lambda_k(p)}}p$
as $x\to\infty$. These follow from the Rankin--Selberg method, and
were obtained in a precise form independently by
Wu--Ye \cite[Thm.~3]{wu-ye} and Avdispahi\'c--Smajlovi\'c \cite[Thm.~2.2]{as}.
(We also make use of similar estimates for sums over $p$ in an arithmetic
progression---see Lemma~\ref{lem:sump} for the exact statement---though
it is likely that this could be avoided at the expense of making the
proof more complicated.)

Since quasi-orthogonality and the Ramanujan conjecture are essentially
the only properties of automorphic $L$-functions that we require,
one could instead take these as hypotheses and state the theorem for
an axiomatically-defined class of $L$-functions, such as the Selberg
class. However, it has been conjectured that the Selberg
class coincides with the class of automorphic $L$-functions, so this
likely offers no greater generality.

\item The conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} is interesting
even for $n=1$. For instance, Nakamura and Pa\'nkowski \cite {np}
have shown very recently, for a wide class of $L$-functions $L(s)$,
that if $P\in R[x]$ is not a monomial and $\delta>0$ then $P(L(s))$
necessarily has zeros in the half-plane $\Re(s)>1-\delta$. Our result
strengthens this to $\Re(s)>1$. (On the other hand,
\cite{np} also yields the estimate \eqref{eqn:Nlowerbound} for any
$[\sigma_1,\sigma_2]\subseteq(\frac12,1)$, which does not follow from
our method.)

\item Our results are related to universality results 
for zeta and $L$-functions. Voronin \cite{voronin} proved for any compact
set $K$ with connected complement contained within the strip $\Re(s) \in (\frac12, 1)$, and any nonvanishing, continuous 
function $f :  K \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ holomorphic on the interior of $K$, that $f$ can be uniformly
approximated by vertical translates of the zeta function. 

Voronin's results were extended
by a number of authors. One result similar to ours, due to
Laurin\v{c}ikas and Matsumoto \cite{LM}, states that given $m$ functions $f_1, \dots, f_m$ as above, and
$L$-functions $L_j(s, F)$ associated to twists of a Hecke newform $F$ by pairwise inequivalent Dirichlet characters, that the $f_j$ may
be simultaneously approximated by a single vertical translate of the functions $L_j(s, F)$.
This implies \cite[Theorem 4]{LM} that non-trivial linear combinations of the $L_j(s, F)$ must
contain zeros inside the critical strip with $\Re(s) > \frac{1}{2}$.

References to many more works on universality can be found in \cite{LM}.

\end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Remarks: non-vanishing on $\Re(s)\ge1$, infinitely many zeros with a lower bound, relaxing Ramanujan, quasi-orthogonality as main tool, the case $n=1$, and universality.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.1 (quasi-orthogonality in arithmetic progressions)
nodes.statement:
\footnote{[Added after publication.] As Mattia Righetti pointed out to us, this lemma is incorrect
as claimed, although the statement is true with $O(\sigma - 1)$ replaced by $O\big( \frac{1}{\log(2/(\sigma - 1))}\big)$. The final
line of the proof does not follow with the uniformity claimed, but in a published correction we prove that the bound
$\sum_{p > y} p^{-\sigma} \gg \frac{y^{1 - \sigma}}{\log y} \log \frac{2}{\sigma - 1}$ does.

The lemma is used in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:sw1}, where it is needed only that the error tend to $0$
as $\sigma \rightarrow 1^+$. The corrected error term is sufficient, and the remaining results remain valid with only
cosmetic changes to the proofs.}
Let $a$ and $q$ be positive integers satisfying
$\bigl(q,a\prod_{j=1}^n\mathrm{cond}(\pi_j)\bigr)=1$.
Then
\[
\sum_{\substack{p>y\\p\equiv{a}\;(\text{\rm mod }q)}}
\frac{|u_1\lambda_1(p)+\ldots+u_n \lambda_n(p)|^2}{p^\sigma} = 
\bigg( \frac{1}{ \phi(q)} + O(\sigma-1)\bigg)
\sum_{p>y}p^{-\sigma}
\]
for all $y>0$, $\sigma\in(1,2]$ and all unit vectors
$(u_1, \ldots, u_n)$, where the implied constant
depends only on $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n$ and $q$.
nodes.statement_short: Rankin-Selberg quasi-orthogonality: weighted sums of $|\sum u_j\lambda_j(p)|^2p^{-\sigma}$ over a progression mod $q$ are $(1/\phi(q)+O(\sigma-1))\sum_{p>y}p^{-\sigma}$.
assumptions: Let $a$ and $q$ be positive integers satisfying $\bigl(q,a\prod_{j=1}^n\mathrm{cond}(\pi_j)\bigr)=1$.
for all $y>0$, $\sigma\in(1,2]$ and all unit vectors $(u_1, \ldots, u_n)$
conclusions: \sum_{\substack{p>y\\p\equiv{a}\;(\text{\rm mod }q)}} \frac{|u_1\lambda_1(p)+\ldots+u_n \lambda_n(p)|^2}{p^\sigma} = \bigg( \frac{1}{ \phi(q)} + O(\sigma-1)\bigg) \sum_{p>y}p^{-\sigma}
nodes.label: lem:sump

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement:
Let $\chi\;(\text{mod }q)$ be a Dirichlet character, not necessarily primitive.
We consider the sum
\[
E_{jk\chi}(x)=
\sum_{p\le x}\big(\lambda_j(p)\overline{\lambda_k(p)}\chi(p)
-\delta_{jk\chi}\big)\frac{\log{p}}{p},
\]
running over primes $p\le x$,
where $\delta_{jk\chi}=1$ if $j=k$ and $\chi$ is the trivial
character, and $0$ otherwise.  Applying \cite[(2) and (3)]{as} with
$(\pi,\pi')=(\pi_j\otimes\chi,\pi_k)$ and, if $\chi$ is imprimitive,
subtracting any contribution from the terms with $p|q$,
we obtain the bound $E_{jk\chi}(x)\ll_q 1$.

Next, for any non-integral $y\ge\frac32$ and any $\sigma\in(1,2]$, we have
$$
\sum_{p>y}
\frac{\lambda_j(p)\overline{\lambda_k(p)}\chi(p)-\delta_{jk\chi}}{p^\sigma}
=\int_y^\infty\frac{t^{1-\sigma}}{\log{t}}\,dE_{jk\chi}(t).
$$
Integrating by parts and applying the above estimate for
$E_{jk\chi}$, we see that this is $\ll_q y^{1-\sigma}/\log{y}$.

Now, expanding the square and using orthogonality of Dirichlet
characters, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{\substack{p>y\\p\equiv{a}\;(\text{mod }q)}}
\frac{|u_1\lambda_1(p)+\ldots+u_n\lambda_n(p)|^2}{p^\sigma}&=
\frac1{\phi(q)}\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^n
\sum_{\chi\;(\text{mod }q)}u_j\overline{u_k}\overline{\chi(a)}
\sum_{p>y}\frac{\lambda_j(p)\overline{\lambda_k(p)}\chi(p)}{p^\sigma}\\
&=O_q\!\left(\frac{y^{1-\sigma}}{\log{y}}\right)
+\frac1{\phi(q)}\sum_{p>y}p^{-\sigma}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Finally, by the prime number theorem we have
$\sum_{p>y}p^{-\sigma}\gg\frac{y^{1-\sigma}}{(\sigma-1)\log{y}}$,
uniformly for $y\ge\frac32$ and $\sigma\in(1,2]$.
The lemma follows.
nodes.statement_short: Bound twisted Rankin-Selberg prime sums via Avdispahic-Smajlovic, integrate by parts, expand the square with character orthogonality, and compare with the prime number theorem.

nodes.name: Matrix space $\mathrm{Mat}_{n\times n}(\mathbb{C})$
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathrm{Mat}_{n\times n}(\mathbb{C})$ denote the set of $n\times n$ matrices with
entries in $\mathbb{C}$.

nodes.name: Frobenius norm
nodes.statement:
For $A=(a_{ij})\in\mathrm{Mat}_{n\times n}(\mathbb{C})$,
the {\itshape Frobenius norm} is defined by
\[
\|A\|=\sqrt{\mathrm{tr}\left(\overline{A}^T A\right)}=\sqrt{\sum|a_{ij}|^2}.
\]

nodes.name: Frobenius norm bounds operator action
nodes.statement:
By the Schwarz inequality, we have
$|Av|\le\|A\|\cdot|v|$ for any $A\in\mathrm{Mat}_{n\times n}(\mathbb{C})$ and $v\in\mathbb{C}^n$.
assumptions: for any $A\in\mathrm{Mat}_{n\times n}(\mathbb{C})$ and $v\in\mathbb{C}^n$
conclusions: $|Av|\le\|A\|\cdot|v|$

nodes.name: $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ with subspace topology
nodes.statement:
We endow $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})=\{g\in\mathrm{Mat}_{n\times n}(\mathbb{C}):\det{g}\ne0\}$
with the subspace topology.

nodes.name: Compactness criterion in $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$
nodes.statement:
In particular,
it is easy to see that a set $K\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ is
compact if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathrm{Mat}_{n\times n}(\mathbb{C})$
and there are positive real numbers $c$ and $C$ such that
$$
\|g\|\le C\text{ and }|\det{g}|\ge c
\quad\text{for all }g\in K.
$$
nodes.statement_short: $K\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ is compact iff closed in matrices with $\|g\|$ bounded above and $|\det g|$ bounded below.
assumptions: a set $K\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$
conclusions: compact if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathrm{Mat}_{n\times n}(\mathbb{C})$ and there are positive real numbers $c$ and $C$ such that

nodes.name: Inverse norm bounded on compact sets
nodes.statement:
Since $g^{-1}$ can be expressed in terms of $\frac1{\det{g}}$ and the
cofactor matrix of $g$, it follows that $\|g^{-1}\|$ is bounded on $K$
(and indeed the map $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ is continuous, so that
$\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ is a topological group with this topology).
assumptions: on $K$
conclusions: $\|g^{-1}\|$ is bounded on $K$

nodes.name: Lemma 2.2 (neighborhood stability)
nodes.statement:
Suppose $K$ is a compact subset of $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$, $g\in K$,
and $U\subseteq\mathbb{C}^n$ contains an open $\delta$-neighborhood of some
point.  Then $gU$ contains an $\varepsilon$-neighborhood,
where $\varepsilon > 0$ depends only on $\delta$ and $K$.
assumptions: Suppose $K$ is a compact subset of $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$, $g\in K$, and $U\subseteq\mathbb{C}^n$ contains an open $\delta$-neighborhood of some point.
conclusions: Then $gU$ contains an $\varepsilon$-neighborhood, where $\varepsilon > 0$ depends only on $\delta$ and $K$.
nodes.label: lem:nbhd_stability

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2
nodes.statement:
By linearity, we may assume without loss of generality that $U$ contains
the $\delta$-neighborhood of the origin, $N_\delta$. Since $K$ is
compact, there is a number $C>0$ such that $\|g^{-1}\|\le C$ for all
$g\in K$.  Put $\varepsilon=C^{-1}\delta$, and let $N_\varepsilon$ be the
$\varepsilon$-neighborhood of the origin. For any $v\in N_\varepsilon$
we have $|g^{-1}v|\le\|g^{-1}\|\cdot|v|<C\varepsilon=\delta$, so that
$v=g(g^{-1}v)\in gN_\delta$. Since $v$ was arbitrary, $gN_\delta\supseteq
N_\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a neighborhood of the origin; bound $\|g^{-1}\|\le C$ on compact $K$ and take $\varepsilon=C^{-1}\delta$.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.3 (square-root cancellation by phases)
nodes.statement:
For any $v_0, \ldots, v_k \in \mathbb{C}^n$, there exist
$\theta_0, \ldots, \theta_k \in [0, 1]$ such that
\[
\left| \sum_{j = 0}^k e(\theta_k) v_j\right| \leq \sqrt{\sum_{j=0}^k|v_j|^2}.
\]
assumptions: For any $v_0, \ldots, v_k \in \mathbb{C}^n$
conclusions: there exist $\theta_0, \ldots, \theta_k \in [0, 1]$ such that \[ \left| \sum_{j = 0}^k e(\theta_k) v_j\right| \leq \sqrt{\sum_{j=0}^k|v_j|^2}. \]
nodes.label: lem:sq_root_avg

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.3
nodes.statement:
We have
\[
\int_{[0, 1]^k}\left|\sum_{j=0}^k e(\theta_j) v_j\right|^2
d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_k = \sum_{j=0}^{k}|v_j|^2.
\]
Thus, the average choice of $(\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_k)$ satisfies the
conclusion.
nodes.statement_short: Averaging argument: the mean square over random phases equals $\sum|v_j|^2$.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.4 (monomial criterion)
nodes.statement:
Let $P\in\mathbb{C}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. Suppose that every solution to the
equation $P(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=0$ satisfies $x_1\cdots x_n=0$.
Then $P$ is a monomial, i.e., $P=cx_1^{d_1}\ldots x_n^{d_n}$ for 
some $c\neq0$ and non-negative integers $d_1,\ldots,d_n$.
assumptions: Let $P\in\mathbb{C}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$.
Suppose that every solution to the equation $P(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=0$ satisfies $x_1\cdots x_n=0$.
conclusions: Then $P$ is a monomial, i.e., $P=cx_1^{d_1}\ldots x_n^{d_n}$ for some $c\neq0$ and non-negative integers $d_1,\ldots,d_n$.
nodes.label: lem:monomial

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.4
nodes.statement:
Let $V=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb{C}^n:P(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=0\}$ be the vanishing
set of $P$. By hypothesis, the polynomial $x_1\cdots x_n$ vanishes on
$V$. Thus, since $\mathbb{C}$ is algebraically closed, Hilbert's Nullstellensatz
implies that there is some $d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$ such that $(x_1\cdots x_n)^d$
is contained in the ideal generated by $P$, i.e.\ $P|(x_1\cdots x_n)^d$.
Since $\mathbb{C}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ is a unique factorization domain,
this is only possible if $P$ is a monomial.
nodes.statement_short: By Hilbert's Nullstellensatz $P$ divides a power of $x_1\cdots x_n$; unique factorization forces $P$ to be a monomial.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.5 (continuity of zeros of polynomials)
nodes.statement:
Let $P\in\mathbb{C}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and
suppose that $y\in\mathbb{C}^n$ is a zero of $P$. Then for any $\varepsilon>0$ there exists
$\delta>0$ such that any polynomial $Q\in\mathbb{C}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, obtained by changing any of the nonzero coefficients
of $P$ by at most $\delta$ each, has a zero $z\in\mathbb{C}^n$ with $|y-z|<\varepsilon$.
assumptions: Let $P\in\mathbb{C}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and suppose that $y\in\mathbb{C}^n$ is a zero of $P$.
conclusions: for any $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\delta>0$ such that any polynomial $Q\in\mathbb{C}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, obtained by changing any of the nonzero coefficients of $P$ by at most $\delta$ each, has a zero $z\in\mathbb{C}^n$ with $|y-z|<\varepsilon$.
nodes.label: lem:poly_cont

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.5
nodes.statement:
If $P$ is identically $0$ then so is $Q$, so we may take $z=y$.
Otherwise, set
$$
p(t)=P(y+tu)\quad\text{and}\quad q(t)=Q(y+tu)
$$
for $t\in\mathbb{C}$, where $u$ is any unit vector for which 
$p(t)$ does not vanish for all $t$; shrinking $\varepsilon$ if necessary, assume that
$p(t)$ does not vanish on $C_\varepsilon=\{t\in\mathbb{C}:|t|=\varepsilon\}$; and
let $\gamma>0$ be the minimum of $|p(t)|$ on $C_\varepsilon$. For
$t\in C_\varepsilon$ we have
\[
|q(t) - p(t)| < \delta N \Big(1+\varepsilon+|y|\Big)^{\deg P}
\]
where $N$ is the number of nonzero coefficients of $P$. 
Choosing $\delta$ so that the right side of this expression is bounded by $\gamma$, we have
$|q(t)-p(t)|<|p(t)|$ for $t\in C_\varepsilon$.
By Rouch\'e's theorem $q(t)$ has a zero $t_0$ of modulus
$|t_0|<\varepsilon$, and taking $z=y+t_0u$ completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to a complex line through $y$ and apply Rouche's theorem on a small circle.

nodes.name: Proposition 3.2 (continuous solution of matrix equations on the torus)
nodes.statement:
Let
\[
T = \{ (z_1, \ldots, z_n) \in \mathbb{C}^n \ : \ |z_1| = \ldots = |z_n| = 1 \},
\]
\[
D = \{ (z_1, \ldots, z_n) \in \mathbb{C}^n \ : \ |z_1|, \ldots, |z_n| \leq 1 \},
\]
and fix a compact set $K \subseteq \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$.
Then there is a number $m_0 > 0$ such that for every $m \geq m_0$ and all
$(g_1, \ldots, g_m) \in K^m$, there are continuous functions
$f_1, \ldots, f_m : D \rightarrow T$ such that
$\sum_{i = 1}^m g_i f_i(z) = z$ for all $z \in D$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers
nodes.statement_short: For $m$ large and any $g_1,\ldots,g_m$ in a compact $K\subset\mathrm{GL}_n$, the polydisc $D$ is continuously parametrized as $\sum g_if_i(z)$ with $f_i(z)$ on the torus.
assumptions: fix a compact set $K \subseteq \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$
conclusions: Then there is a number $m_0 > 0$ such that for every $m \geq m_0$ and all $(g_1, \ldots, g_m) \in K^m$, there are continuous functions $f_1, \ldots, f_m : D \rightarrow T$ such that $\sum_{i = 1}^m g_i f_i(z) = z$ for all $z \in D$.
nodes.label: prop:td

nodes.name: Three-step plan of the proof of Proposition 3.2
nodes.statement:
We will carry out the proof in three steps:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item We first show that there exist $\varepsilon > 0$ and
$m_1$ such that
for all $m \geq m_1$ and all $(g_1, \ldots, g_m) \in K^m$, the set
$\{ \sum_{i = 1}^m g_i t_i : t_1,\ldots,t_m \in T \}$
contains an open $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of a point in $\mathbb{C}^n$.
\item `Fattening' the neighborhood constructed in the first step, we will 
show that there exists $m_2$ such that for $m \geq m_2$ and all
$(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\in K^m$,
$\{ \sum_{i = 1}^m g_i t_i : t_1,\ldots,t_m \in T \}$
contains the closed ball of radius $2$,
$\{(z_1,\ldots,z_n):|z_1|^2+\ldots+|z_n|^2\le4\}$.
\item Although the previous step yields a parametrization of a large closed
set, it is not
obviously continuous. By repeating the construction from step
\eqref{it_small_neigh} using the added knowledge of step \eqref{it_big_neigh},
we show that one can achieve a continuous parametrization of $D$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers
nodes.statement_short: Plan: (1) a small neighborhood in the image, (2) fattening to the ball of radius 2, (3) a continuous parametrization of $D$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.2
nodes.statement:
We begin by showing \eqref{it_small_neigh}. By compactness, 
there is an $m_1$ such that for any $m\ge m_1$ and any $m$-tuple
$(g_1, \ldots, g_m)$, there is a distinct pair of indices $i,j$
such that $\| g_i^{-1} g_j - I \| < \frac{1}{3 \sqrt{n}}$.
Assume, without loss of generality, that $(i,j)=(1,2)$, and
put $\Delta = g_1^{-1} g_2 - I$. Then for any choice of $t_1, t_2 \in T$,
we have
\[
g_1 t_1 + g_2 t_2 = g_1 (t_1 + (I + \Delta) t_2),
\]
where $\| \Delta \|<\frac1{3\sqrt{n}}$.

We introduce some notation. First, define $A=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z-1|\le\frac13\}$
and $B=\{ z \in \mathbb{C} : |z - 1| \leq \frac{2}{3} \}$.
Next, let $s_1, s_2: B \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be the unique continuous
functions satisfying $z = s_1(z) + s_2(z)$,
$|s_1(z)| = |s_2(z)| = 1$ and $\Im(\frac{s_1(z)}{s_2(z)}) > 0$ for all
$z\in B$. For $j=1,2$, let $t_j:B^n\rightarrow T$ be defined by
$t_j(z_1,\ldots,z_n)=(s_j(z_1),\ldots,s_j(z_n))$.

Given an arbitrary element $w\in A^n$,
we define a continuous function $h_w: B^n \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^n$ by
$h_w(z) = w - \Delta{t_2(z)}$.
Since $|t_2(z)|=\sqrt{n}$ and
$\|\Delta\|<\frac1{3\sqrt{n}}$, we have
$|\Delta t_2(z)|<\frac13$.
In particular, each entry of $\Delta t_2(z)$ is bounded in magnitude
by $\frac13$, so by the triangle inequality, the
image of $h_w$ is contained in $B^n$. By the Brouwer fixed point theorem,
there exists $z \in B^n$ with $h_w(z) = z$, so that
\[
t_1(z) + (I + \Delta) t_2(z) = z+\Delta{t_2(z)} = z+w-h_w(z) = w.
\]
Therefore, all of $A^n$ is in the image of the map
$z \mapsto t_1(z) + (I + \Delta) t_2(z)$,
so that in particular
\[
A^n \subseteq \{ t_1 + g_1^{-1} g_2 t_2 \ : \ t_1, t_2 \in T \}.
\]

Applying Lemma \ref{lem:nbhd_stability} with $\delta=\frac13$,
there is an $\varepsilon>0$
depending only on $K$ such that
$\{ g_1 t_1 + g_2 t_2 \ : \ t_1, t_2 \in T \}$ 
contains an $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of some point in $\mathbb{C}^n$.
We conclude the same of the set
$\{ g_1 t_1 + \ldots + g_m t_m \ : \ t_1, \ldots, t_m \in T \}$
by choosing arbitrary fixed $t_3, \ldots, t_m \in T$.
\\
\\
Proceeding to step \eqref{it_big_neigh}, let $k_1$ be a large integer
to be determined later, set $m_2 = m_1 k_1$, and for any $m \geq m_2$ write
$m = k m_1 + l$ 
with $k\ge k_1$ and
$0 \leq l < m_1$.

For each $j$ with $0\leq j<k$, applying step \eqref{it_small_neigh}
to $(g_{jm_1+1},\ldots,g_{jm_1+m_1})$, we obtain an $\varepsilon$-neighborhood
centered at some $v_j\in \mathbb{C}^n$. Further, we put
$v_k = g_{km_1 + 1} \overrightarrow{1} + \ldots
+ g_{k m_1 + l} \overrightarrow{1}$, where
$\overrightarrow{1} = (1, \ldots, 1) \in T$.
Since $m_1$ is fixed and $K$ is compact, 
we have $|v_j| \leq C$ for $0\leq j\leq k$, for some $C$ independent of the individual $g_i$.

Let
$N_\varepsilon=\{(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in\mathbb{C}^n:|z_1|^2+\ldots+|z_n|^2<\varepsilon^2\}$
be the $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of the origin in $\mathbb{C}^n$. Then by the
above observations, for any $\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_k\in[0,1]$,
$\big\{ \sum_{i = 1}^m g_i t_i \, : \, t_1,\ldots,t_m \in T \big\}$
contains the set
$$
\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e( \theta_j)(v_j+N_{\varepsilon})+e(\theta_k)v_k
=\sum_{j=0}^ke(\theta_j)v_j+kN_{\varepsilon}.
$$
By Lemma~\ref{lem:sq_root_avg}, there is a choice of
$\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_k$ for which
$\bigl|\sum_{j=0}^ke(\theta_j)v_j\bigr|\le C\sqrt{k+1}$.
Now let $k_1$ be the smallest positive integer satisfying
$k_1\varepsilon > C \sqrt{k_1 + 1} + 2$. Then for $k\ge k_1$, we have
shown that $\{ \sum_{i = 1}^m g_i t_i : t_1,\ldots,t_m\in T \}$
contains the closed ball of radius $2$.
\\
\\
Proceeding to step \eqref{it_cont}, we put $m_0=3nm_2$. Suppose that 
$m\geq m_0$ and $(g_1,\dots,g_m)$ are given, and choose a partition
of $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ into $3n$
sets $I_{j,\ell}$ (for $1\leq j\leq n$, $1\leq \ell\leq3$),
each of size at least $m_2$.
For each $j$ with $1\leq j\leq n$, write
\[
v_j = v_{j,1} = v_{j,2} = v_{j,3} = (0,\ldots,0,2,0,\ldots,0),
\]
where the $2$ is in the $j$th position. For each $j$ and $\ell$ we use
step \eqref{it_big_neigh} to express $v_{j,\ell}$ in the form
\begin{equation} v_{j,\ell} = \sum_{i\in I_{j,\ell}}g_i t_i
\end{equation}
for some $t_i\in T$.

Next, note that the set
$\bigl\{2[(1,\ldots,1)+\alpha+\beta]\ : \alpha,\beta\in T\}$
contains $D$. As in the proof of step \eqref{it_small_neigh},
we can choose continuous functions
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n), \beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n):D\to T$
such that
$z_j=2[1+\alpha_j(z)+\beta_j(z)]$ for every $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in D$.
Thus,
$$
z=\sum_{j=1}^n[1+\alpha_j(z)+\beta_j(z)]v_j
=\sum_{j=1}^n [v_{j,1}+\alpha_j(z)v_{j,2}+\beta_j(z)v_{j,3}].
$$
Finally, we use \eqref{eqn:step3_idecomp} to rewrite this as
$$
z=\sum_{j=1}^n\left[
\sum_{i\in I_{j,1}}g_it_i 
+\sum_{i\in I_{j,2}}g_i\big(t_i\alpha_j(z)\big)
+\sum_{i\in I_{j,3}}g_i\big(t_i\beta_j(z)\big)\right],
$$
which is a decomposition of the type required.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers
nodes.statement_short: Three steps: a Brouwer fixed point argument gives a small neighborhood, random phases (Lemma 2.3) fatten it to the radius-2 ball, then a coordinate decomposition gives a continuous parametrization. Key step: the fixed point of $h_w(z)=w-\Delta t_2(z)$.

nodes.name: Decomposition (3.1)
nodes.statement: v_{j,\ell} = \sum_{i\in I_{j,\ell}}g_i t_i

nodes.statement:
Given a real parameter $y>0$, we write
\[
S(y) = \{p \text{ prime}: p > y \}
\quad\text{and}\quad
s(y,\sigma) = \sum_{p\in S(y)} p^{-\sigma}.
\]

There is a compact set $K \subseteq \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$, explicitly defined in \eqref{eqn:def_K}
depending only on the
degrees $r_1,\ldots,r_n$, with the following property:

Let $m$ be a positive integer. Then there is a real number
$\delta>0$ (depending on the $\pi_j$ and $m$) such that for any $y>0$
and any $\sigma\in(1,1+\delta]$,
there exists a partition of $S(y)$ into $mn$ pairwise disjoint subsets

\end{equation}
lies in $K^m$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.3
nodes.statement:
Let $q$ be the smallest prime number satisfying $q\equiv1\pmod{mn}$ and
$q\nmid\prod_{j=1}^n\mathrm{cond}(\pi_j)$. We put $t=\frac{q-1}{mn}$ and
define $S_{ik}^\circ(y)$ to be the union of residue classes
$$
S_{ik}^\circ(y)=\bigcup_{\ell=1}^t
\bigl\{p\in S(y):p\equiv tn(i-1)+t(k-1)+\ell\pmod{q}\bigr\},
$$
and
$$
S_{ik}(y)=\begin{cases}
S_{ik}^\circ(y)\cup\{q\}&\text{if }
i=k=1\text{ and }y<q,\\
S_{ik}^\circ(y)&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
Then the $S_{ik}(y)$ are pairwise disjoint and cover $S(y)$.

For a fixed choice of $i$, let $v_k$ denote the $k$th column of $g_i$,
as defined in \eqref{eqn:gidef}, with the $\epsilon_p$ yet to be chosen.
We will show by induction that there is a choice of the $\epsilon_p$ such that
\begin{equation} |v_\ell - \mathrm{proj}_{\mathrm{span}\{v_1, \ldots, v_{\ell - 1}\}} v_\ell| \geq
\frac{1}{2r}
\end{equation}
holds for every $\ell=1,\ldots,n$, where $r=\sqrt{r_1^2+\ldots+r_n^2}$.
To that end,
let $k$ be given, and assume that \eqref{eqn:projspan} has been
established for $\ell=1,\ldots,k-1$.  Choose a unit vector
$u = (u_1, \ldots, u_n)$ orthogonal to $v_1, \ldots, v_{k - 1}$.
By the Schwarz inequality and the Ramanujan bound
$|\lambda_j(p)|\le r_j$, for each prime $p$ we have
$
|\bar{u}_1 \lambda_1(p) + \ldots + \bar{u}_n \lambda_n(p)| \leq
r.
$
Therefore
\begin{align} \frac{mn}{s(y, \sigma)}
\sum_{p\in S_{ik}(y)}
\frac{|\bar{u}_1\lambda_1(p)+\ldots+\bar{u}_n\lambda_n(p)|}{p^\sigma}
&\geq\frac{mn}{r s(y, \sigma)} \sum_{p\in S_{ik}^\circ(y)}
\frac{|\bar{u}_1\lambda_1(p)+\ldots+\bar{u}_n\lambda_n(p)|^2}{p^\sigma}\\
&=\frac{1+O_{m, n}(\sigma-1)}{r}, \nonumber
\end{align}
the latter equality following by Lemma \ref{lem:sump}.
We choose $\delta$ so that the $O$ term
above is bounded in modulus by $\frac12$, and
for each $p \in S_{ik}(y)$ we choose $\epsilon_p$ such that
$\epsilon_p (\bar{u}_1 \lambda_1(p) + \ldots + \bar{u}_n \lambda_n(p))$
is real and nonnegative. Then 
the left side of \eqref{eqn:inn_prod} equals
\[
\langle u, v_k \rangle = 
\langle u, v_k - \mathrm{proj}_{\mathrm{span}\{v_1, \ldots, v_{k - 1}\}} v_k \rangle \leq
|v_k - \mathrm{proj}_{\mathrm{span}\{v_1, \ldots, v_{k - 1}\}} v_k|,
\]
so that \eqref{eqn:projspan} follows for $\ell=k$.

Applying Gram--Schmidt orthogonalization to $v_1,\ldots,v_n$, it follows
from \eqref{eqn:projspan} that
$|\det{g_i}|\ge (2r)^{-n}$. Moreover, by the Schwarz inequality
and Lemma \ref{lem:sump} again, each entry of $g_i$ is bounded above by
$1+O_{m, n}(\sigma-1)$,
so that $\|g_i\|\le2n$ for a suitable choice of $\delta$. Thus,
\begin{equation} K=\{g\in\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C}):\|g\|\le 2n, |\det{g}|\ge(2r)^{-n}\}
\end{equation}
has the desired properties.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement:
We use Propositions \ref{prop:sw1} and \ref{prop:td} to 
determine a compact set $K\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$, a positive integer
$m_0$, and a real number $\delta>0$ with the properties described
there. 
Taking $m=m_0$,
the aforementioned propositions yield, for any
$\sigma\in(1,1+\delta]$, an $m$-tuple of matrices
$(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\in K^m$, elements $\epsilon_p \in S^1$ for each prime $p > y$, and
continuous functions $f_1,\dots,f_m:D\rightarrow T$
such that
\begin{equation} \sum_{i=1}^m g_i f_i(z) = z\quad\text{for all }z\in D.
\end{equation}

Now, let $\mu=\frac{s(y,\sigma)}{mn}$.
For each prime $p>y$, we define
a continuous function $t_p : \mu D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ satisfying
\begin{equation} p^{- i t_p(z)} = \epsilon_p f_i(\mu^{-1}z)_k,
\end{equation}
where $(i,k)$ is the unique pair of indices for which $p\in S_{ik}(y)$ and
$f_i(\mu^{-1}z)_k$ denotes the $k$th component of
$f_i(\mu^{-1}z)$.
(Note that the lift from $S^1$ to $\mathbb{R}$ is
possible since $D$ is simply connected.)

Define an error term $E(z)=(E_1(z),\ldots,E_n(z))$ by writing,
for each $j=1,\ldots,n$, 
$$
E_j(z)=\sum_{p>y}\left(\log L(\sigma+it_p(z),\pi_{j,p}) 
-\lambda_j(p)p^{-(\sigma+it_p(z))}\right).
$$
By the Ramanujan bound, we have
$$
\log L(s,\pi_{j,p})-\lambda_j(p)p^{-s}=O(p^{-2})
$$
uniformly for $\Re(s)\ge1$. Since $\sum_p p^{-2}$ converges,
the continuity of $E$ follows from that of the individual $t_p$.
Moreover, each component $E_j(z)$ is bounded by a number $C>0$, independent
of $j$, $z$, $y$, or $\sigma$. 

Set $R'=\sqrt{\pi^2+\log^2{R}}$.  We take $\eta\in(0,\delta]$
small enough that the condition $\sigma\in(1,1+\eta]$ ensures that
$\mu\ge C+R'$.
By \eqref{eqn:id_decomp}, \eqref{eqn:def_tp}, and
Proposition \ref{prop:sw1} we have
$$
\sum_{p>y}\lambda_j(p)p^{-(\sigma+it_p(z))}=
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{k=1}^n
\sum_{p\in S_{ik}(y)} 
\frac{\lambda_j(p)\epsilon_pf_i(\mu^{-1}z)_k}{p^{\sigma}}=z_j,
$$
for any $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in\mu{D}$.
Now fix $w\in R'D$ and define a function
$F_w:(C+R')D\to\mathbb{C}$ by $F_w(z)=w-E(z)$.
By the estimate for $E_j(z)$ above, the image of $F_w$ is contained
in $(C+R')D$. Thus,
by the Brouwer fixed point theorem, there exists $z\in(C+R')D$
with $F_w(z)=z$, so that
\[
\biggl(\sum_{p>y}\log L(\sigma+it_p(z),\pi_{j,p})\biggr)_{j=1,\ldots,n}
=z+E(z)=z+w-F_w(z)=w.
\]
Taking exponentials yields the proposition.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement:
The proof will be carried out in two steps:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item
Applying our previous results, we
show that unless $P$ is a monomial (as described in Theorem \ref{thm:main}), 
for every $\sigma > 1$ sufficiently close to $1$
there are real numbers $t_p$ (for each prime $p$) and $t_0$ 
such that $P|_{s=\sigma+it_0}$
vanishes at $\bigl(\prod_pL(\sigma+it_p,\pi_{1,p}),\ldots,
\prod_pL(\sigma+it_p,\pi_{n,p})\bigr)$.
\item Simultaneously approximating the $p^{-it_p}$ by $p^{-it}$ for a
common value of $t$, we use Rouch\'e's theorem to find a zero of
$P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ close to $\sigma+it$.
\end{enumerate}
Note that the second step is standard and is applied in \cite{SW}
in much the same way.
\\
\\
We begin with a polynomial $P$ whose coefficients are 
finite Dirichlet series $D(s)=\sum_{m=1}^M a_mm^{-s}$, and let
$y$ be the largest value of $M$ occurring in any of these coefficients.
We rewrite each $L(s,\pi_j)$ as
$L_{\leq{y}}(s,\pi_j)L_{>y}(s,\pi_j)$,
splitting each Euler product into products over primes $p\leq y$
and $p>y$ respectively. Setting
$$
Q(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
=P\bigl(L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_1)x_1,\ldots,L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_n)x_n\bigr),
$$
we have
$P(L(s,\pi_1),\dots,L(s,\pi_n))=Q(L_{>y}(s,\pi_1),\dots,L_{>y}(s,\pi_n))$.

The coefficients of $Q$ are rational functions of
the $p^{-s}$ for $p\le y$.  More precisely, for any monomial term
$D(s)x_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ in the expansion of $P$, the corresponding
term of $Q$ is 
\[D(s)L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_1)^{d_1}\cdots{}L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_n)^{d_n}
x_1^{d_1}\cdots{}x_n^{d_n}.
\]  Since the finite
Euler products $L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_j)$ are non-vanishing holomorphic functions
on $\{s\in\mathbb{C}:\Re(s)\ge1\}$, the corresponding terms of $P$ and $Q$
have the same zeros there.

Let $D_1(s),\ldots,D_m(s)$ run through the coefficients of $P$ which do
not vanish identically, and consider their product
$f(s)=D_1(s)\cdots D_m(s)$. Then $f$ is itself a finite Dirichlet series
which does not vanish identically. By complex analysis, $f$ cannot
vanish at $1+it$ for every $t\in\mathbb{R}$, so there is some $t_0$
for which $D_1(1+it_0),\ldots,D_m(1+it_0)$ are all non-zero, and the same holds for the corresponding terms of $Q$.

Next we 
specialize the coefficients of $Q$ to a fixed value of $s$, obtaining
a polynomial $h_s\in\mathbb{C}[x_1,\dots,x_n]$. Considering $s=1+it_0$, Lemma \ref{lem:monomial}
implies that either $h_{1+it_0}=cx_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$
for some $c\in\mathbb{C}$
and $d_1,\ldots,d_n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$, or that there are $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb{C}$,
none zero, for which $h_{1+it_0}(y_1,\ldots,y_n)=0$.
In the former case, it follows from our choice of $t_0$ that
$P=D(s)x_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ is a monomial, as allowed in the
conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
Henceforth we assume that we are in the latter case,
and aim to show that $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$
has a zero with $\Re(s)>1$.

We choose $R>1$ so that $R^{-{1/2}}\leq|y_j|\leq R^{1/2}$ for
every $j$.  By Lemma \ref{lem:poly_cont}, there is a number
$\varepsilon>0$ such that for every $\sigma\in(1,1+\varepsilon]$,
there exists $(z_1(\sigma),\ldots,z_n(\sigma))\in\mathbb{C}^n$
satisfying $h_{\sigma+it_0}(z_1(\sigma),\ldots,z_n(\sigma))=0$
and $R^{-1}\leq|z_j(\sigma)|\leq R$ for every $j$.  We use
Proposition \ref{prop:lem2} to determine $\eta$ in terms of
$y$ and $R$, and assume that $\eta \le \varepsilon$
by shrinking $\eta$ if necessary.
Proposition~\ref{prop:lem2} then guarantees that, for every
$\sigma\in(1,1+\eta]$, we can solve the
simultaneous system of equations
$$
\prod_{p>y}L(\sigma+it_p,\pi_{j,p})=z_j(\sigma),\quad j=1,\ldots,n,
$$
in the $t_p$ for $p>y$. For $p\le y$ we set $t_p=t_0$, thereby
completing step (1).
\\
\\
Turning to step (2), let $\sigma_1,\sigma_2\in\mathbb{R}$ with
$1<\sigma_1<\sigma_2\le1+\eta$, and put $\sigma=\frac{\sigma_1+\sigma_2}2$.
With the $t_0$ and $t_p$ resulting from step (1) for this choice of $\sigma$,
let $P_{it_0}$ denote the polynomial obtained from $P$ by replacing $s$
by $s+it_0$ in all of its coefficients, and define
\begin{equation} F(s)=P_{it_0}\!\left(
\prod_pL(s+it_p,\pi_{1,p}),\ldots,\prod_pL(s+it_p,\pi_{n,p})\right).
\end{equation}
Then $F$ is holomorphic for $|s-\sigma|<\sigma-1$ and satisfies
$F(\sigma)=0$ by construction. It follows that there
is a number $\rho\in(0,\frac{\sigma_2-\sigma_1}2]$ such that
$F(s)\neq0$ for all $s\in C_\rho=\{s\in\mathbb{C}:|s-\sigma|=\rho\}$.
Write $\gamma$ for the minimum of $|F(s)|$ on $C_\rho$.

Next, by abuse of notation, we write $P(s)$ as shorthand for
$P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$. As
$P(s)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty a_mm^{-s}$ converges absolutely as a Dirichlet
series for $\Re(s) > 1$, there is an integer
$M > 0$ with
$\sum_{m=M}^{\infty}|a_m|m^{-\sigma_1}\le\frac{\gamma}3$.
By \eqref{eqn:Fdef} we have
$F(s)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty b_mm^{-s}$, where
$b_m=a_m\prod_{p|m}p^{-it_p\mathrm{ord}_p(m)}$, and
by the joint uniform distribution of $p^{it}$ for primes $p<M$, it
follows that the set of $t\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfying
\[\sum_{m=1}^{M-1}\frac{|a_mm^{-it}-b_m|}{m^{\sigma_1}}<\frac{\gamma}3\]
has positive lower density.  For any such $t$ the triangle
inequality yields $|P(s+it)-F(s)|<\gamma$ for all $s$ with
$\Re(s)\ge\sigma_1$, and in particular for all $s\in C_\rho$.
By Rouch\'e's theorem, it follows that $P(s+it)$
has a zero $s$ with $|s-\sigma|<\rho$.
Thus, $P(s)$ has zeros with real part in $[\sigma_1,\sigma_2]$, and indeed we have
$$
\#\{s\in\mathbb{C}:\Re(s)\in[\sigma_1,\sigma_2],
\Im(s)\in[-T,T], P(s)=0\}
\gg_{\sigma_1,\sigma_2}T
$$
for all $T\ge T_0(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a non-monomial specialization, use Proposition 3.1 to find shifts $t_p$ giving a zero of an Euler-product model, then simultaneous approximation (Kronecker/Weyl) and Rouche's theorem give genuine zeros.

nodes.name: Definition of $F$ (4.1)
nodes.statement:
F(s)=P_{it_0}\!\left(
\prod_pL(s+it_p,\pi_{1,p}),\ldots,\prod_pL(s+it_p,\pi_{n,p})\right).
nodes.label: eqn:Fdef

nodes.name: Twisted Rankin-Selberg sum
nodes.statement:
Let $\chi\;(\text{mod }q)$ be a Dirichlet character, not necessarily primitive.
We consider the sum
\[
E_{jk\chi}(x)=
\sum_{p\le x}\big(\lambda_j(p)\overline{\lambda_k(p)}\chi(p)
-\delta_{jk\chi}\big)\frac{\log{p}}{p},
\]
running over primes $p\le x$,
where $\delta_{jk\chi}=1$ if $j=k$ and $\chi$ is the trivial
character, and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the twisted prime sum $E_{jk\chi}(x)$.

nodes.name: Bound via Avdispahic-Smajlovic
nodes.statement:
Applying \cite[(2) and (3)]{as} with
$(\pi,\pi')=(\pi_j\otimes\chi,\pi_k)$ and, if $\chi$ is imprimitive,
subtracting any contribution from the terms with $p|q$,
we obtain the bound $E_{jk\chi}(x)\ll_q 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Cite Avdispahic-Smajlovic to get $E_{jk\chi}(x)\ll_q1$.

nodes.name: Partial summation
nodes.statement:
Next, for any non-integral $y\ge\frac32$ and any $\sigma\in(1,2]$, we have
$$
\sum_{p>y}
\frac{\lambda_j(p)\overline{\lambda_k(p)}\chi(p)-\delta_{jk\chi}}{p^\sigma}
=\int_y^\infty\frac{t^{1-\sigma}}{\log{t}}\,dE_{jk\chi}(t).
$$
Integrating by parts and applying the above estimate for
$E_{jk\chi}$, we see that this is $\ll_q y^{1-\sigma}/\log{y}$.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate by parts to bound the tail sum.

nodes.name: Expand and use orthogonality
nodes.statement_short: Expand the square and apply orthogonality of characters.

nodes.name: Compare with prime number theorem
nodes.statement:
Finally, by the prime number theorem we have
$\sum_{p>y}p^{-\sigma}\gg\frac{y^{1-\sigma}}{(\sigma-1)\log{y}}$,
uniformly for $y\ge\frac32$ and $\sigma\in(1,2]$.
The lemma follows.
nodes.statement_short: Use the prime number theorem to absorb the error term.

nodes.name: Reduce to origin
nodes.statement:
By linearity, we may assume without loss of generality that $U$ contains
the $\delta$-neighborhood of the origin, $N_\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $U$ contains the $\delta$-neighborhood of the origin.

nodes.name: Bound inverse norms
nodes.statement:
Since $K$ is
compact, there is a number $C>0$ such that $\|g^{-1}\|\le C$ for all
$g\in K$.
nodes.statement_short: Compactness bounds $\|g^{-1}\|\le C$.

nodes.name: Choose epsilon and check containment
nodes.statement:
Put $\varepsilon=C^{-1}\delta$, and let $N_\varepsilon$ be the
$\varepsilon$-neighborhood of the origin. For any $v\in N_\varepsilon$
we have $|g^{-1}v|\le\|g^{-1}\|\cdot|v|<C\varepsilon=\delta$, so that
$v=g(g^{-1}v)\in gN_\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $\varepsilon=C^{-1}\delta$ and show each $v\in N_\varepsilon$ lies in $gN_\delta$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement:
Since $v$ was arbitrary, $gN_\delta\supseteq
N_\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $gN_\delta\supseteq N_\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Vanishing set
nodes.statement:
Let $V=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb{C}^n:P(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=0\}$ be the vanishing
set of $P$. By hypothesis, the polynomial $x_1\cdots x_n$ vanishes on
$V$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the vanishing set $V$ on which $x_1\cdots x_n$ vanishes.

nodes.name: Nullstellensatz
nodes.statement:
Thus, since $\mathbb{C}$ is algebraically closed, Hilbert's Nullstellensatz
implies that there is some $d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$ such that $(x_1\cdots x_n)^d$
is contained in the ideal generated by $P$, i.e.\ $P|(x_1\cdots x_n)^d$.
nodes.statement_short: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz gives $P\mid(x_1\cdots x_n)^d$.

nodes.name: Unique factorization
nodes.statement:
Since $\mathbb{C}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ is a unique factorization domain,
this is only possible if $P$ is a monomial.
nodes.statement_short: Unique factorization forces $P$ to be a monomial.

nodes.name: Case P identically zero
nodes.statement: If $P$ is identically $0$ then so is $Q$, so we may take $z=y$.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial case $P\equiv0$.

nodes.name: Case P nonzero
nodes.statement:
Otherwise, set
$$
p(t)=P(y+tu)\quad\text{and}\quad q(t)=Q(y+tu)
$$
for $t\in\mathbb{C}$, where $u$ is any unit vector for which 
$p(t)$ does not vanish for all $t$; shrinking $\varepsilon$ if necessary, assume that
$p(t)$ does not vanish on $C_\varepsilon=\{t\in\mathbb{C}:|t|=\varepsilon\}$; and
let $\gamma>0$ be the minimum of $|p(t)|$ on $C_\varepsilon$. For
$t\in C_\varepsilon$ we have
\[
|q(t) - p(t)| < \delta N \Big(1+\varepsilon+|y|\Big)^{\deg P}
\]
where $N$ is the number of nonzero coefficients of $P$. 
Choosing $\delta$ so that the right side of this expression is bounded by $\gamma$, we have
$|q(t)-p(t)|<|p(t)|$ for $t\in C_\varepsilon$.
By Rouch\'e's theorem $q(t)$ has a zero $t_0$ of modulus
$|t_0|<\varepsilon$, and taking $z=y+t_0u$ completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Nonzero case: restrict to a line and apply Rouche.

nodes.name: Restrict to a line
nodes.statement:
Otherwise, set
$$
p(t)=P(y+tu)\quad\text{and}\quad q(t)=Q(y+tu)
$$
for $t\in\mathbb{C}$, where $u$ is any unit vector for which 
$p(t)$ does not vanish for all $t$; shrinking $\varepsilon$ if necessary, assume that
$p(t)$ does not vanish on $C_\varepsilon=\{t\in\mathbb{C}:|t|=\varepsilon\}$; and
let $\gamma>0$ be the minimum of $|p(t)|$ on $C_\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict $P,Q$ to a complex line through $y$; let $\gamma$ be the minimum of $|p|$ on a circle.

nodes.name: Coefficient perturbation bound
nodes.statement:
For
$t\in C_\varepsilon$ we have
\[
|q(t) - p(t)| < \delta N \Big(1+\varepsilon+|y|\Big)^{\deg P}
\]
where $N$ is the number of nonzero coefficients of $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|q-p|$ on the circle in terms of $\delta$.

nodes.name: Choose delta
nodes.statement:
Choosing $\delta$ so that the right side of this expression is bounded by $\gamma$, we have
$|q(t)-p(t)|<|p(t)|$ for $t\in C_\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\delta$ so that $|q-p|<|p|$ on the circle.

nodes.name: Rouche
nodes.statement:
By Rouch\'e's theorem $q(t)$ has a zero $t_0$ of modulus
$|t_0|<\varepsilon$, and taking $z=y+t_0u$ completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Rouche's theorem gives a nearby zero.

nodes.name: Step (1): small neighborhood
nodes.statement:
We begin by showing \eqref{it_small_neigh}. By compactness, 
there is an $m_1$ such that for any $m\ge m_1$ and any $m$-tuple
$(g_1, \ldots, g_m)$, there is a distinct pair of indices $i,j$
such that $\| g_i^{-1} g_j - I \| < \frac{1}{3 \sqrt{n}}$.
Assume, without loss of generality, that $(i,j)=(1,2)$, and
put $\Delta = g_1^{-1} g_2 - I$. Then for any choice of $t_1, t_2 \in T$,
we have
\[
g_1 t_1 + g_2 t_2 = g_1 (t_1 + (I + \Delta) t_2),
\]
where $\| \Delta \|<\frac1{3\sqrt{n}}$.

We introduce some notation. First, define $A=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z-1|\le\frac13\}$
and $B=\{ z \in \mathbb{C} : |z - 1| \leq \frac{2}{3} \}$.
Next, let $s_1, s_2: B \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be the unique continuous
functions satisfying $z = s_1(z) + s_2(z)$,
$|s_1(z)| = |s_2(z)| = 1$ and $\Im(\frac{s_1(z)}{s_2(z)}) > 0$ for all
$z\in B$. For $j=1,2$, let $t_j:B^n\rightarrow T$ be defined by
$t_j(z_1,\ldots,z_n)=(s_j(z_1),\ldots,s_j(z_n))$.

Given an arbitrary element $w\in A^n$,
we define a continuous function $h_w: B^n \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^n$ by
$h_w(z) = w - \Delta{t_2(z)}$.
Since $|t_2(z)|=\sqrt{n}$ and
$\|\Delta\|<\frac1{3\sqrt{n}}$, we have
$|\Delta t_2(z)|<\frac13$.
In particular, each entry of $\Delta t_2(z)$ is bounded in magnitude
by $\frac13$, so by the triangle inequality, the
image of $h_w$ is contained in $B^n$. By the Brouwer fixed point theorem,
there exists $z \in B^n$ with $h_w(z) = z$, so that
\[
t_1(z) + (I + \Delta) t_2(z) = z+\Delta{t_2(z)} = z+w-h_w(z) = w.
\]
Therefore, all of $A^n$ is in the image of the map
$z \mapsto t_1(z) + (I + \Delta) t_2(z)$,
so that in particular
\[
A^n \subseteq \{ t_1 + g_1^{-1} g_2 t_2 \ : \ t_1, t_2 \in T \}.
\]

Applying Lemma \ref{lem:nbhd_stability} with $\delta=\frac13$,
there is an $\varepsilon>0$
depending only on $K$ such that
$\{ g_1 t_1 + g_2 t_2 \ : \ t_1, t_2 \in T \}$ 
contains an $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of some point in $\mathbb{C}^n$.
We conclude the same of the set
$\{ g_1 t_1 + \ldots + g_m t_m \ : \ t_1, \ldots, t_m \in T \}$
by choosing arbitrary fixed $t_3, \ldots, t_m \in T$.
nodes.statement_short: Show the image contains an $\varepsilon$-neighborhood.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Pigeonhole by compactness
nodes.statement:
We begin by showing \eqref{it_small_neigh}. By compactness, 
there is an $m_1$ such that for any $m\ge m_1$ and any $m$-tuple
$(g_1, \ldots, g_m)$, there is a distinct pair of indices $i,j$
such that $\| g_i^{-1} g_j - I \| < \frac{1}{3 \sqrt{n}}$.
nodes.statement_short: By compactness two of the $g_i$ are nearly proportional.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: WLOG and Delta
nodes.statement:
Assume, without loss of generality, that $(i,j)=(1,2)$, and
put $\Delta = g_1^{-1} g_2 - I$. Then for any choice of $t_1, t_2 \in T$,
we have
\[
g_1 t_1 + g_2 t_2 = g_1 (t_1 + (I + \Delta) t_2),
\]
where $\| \Delta \|<\frac1{3\sqrt{n}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $g_1t_1+g_2t_2=g_1(t_1+(I+\Delta)t_2)$ with small $\Delta$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Notation A, B, s_j, t_j
nodes.statement:
We introduce some notation. First, define $A=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z-1|\le\frac13\}$
and $B=\{ z \in \mathbb{C} : |z - 1| \leq \frac{2}{3} \}$.
Next, let $s_1, s_2: B \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be the unique continuous
functions satisfying $z = s_1(z) + s_2(z)$,
$|s_1(z)| = |s_2(z)| = 1$ and $\Im(\frac{s_1(z)}{s_2(z)}) > 0$ for all
$z\in B$. For $j=1,2$, let $t_j:B^n\rightarrow T$ be defined by
$t_j(z_1,\ldots,z_n)=(s_j(z_1),\ldots,s_j(z_n))$.
nodes.statement_short: Define discs $A,B$ and continuous unit-modulus splittings $s_1,s_2$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Map h_w maps into B^n
nodes.statement:
Given an arbitrary element $w\in A^n$,
we define a continuous function $h_w: B^n \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^n$ by
$h_w(z) = w - \Delta{t_2(z)}$.
Since $|t_2(z)|=\sqrt{n}$ and
$\|\Delta\|<\frac1{3\sqrt{n}}$, we have
$|\Delta t_2(z)|<\frac13$.
In particular, each entry of $\Delta t_2(z)$ is bounded in magnitude
by $\frac13$, so by the triangle inequality, the
image of $h_w$ is contained in $B^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $h_w$ and show it maps $B^n$ into itself.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Brouwer fixed point
nodes.statement:
By the Brouwer fixed point theorem,
there exists $z \in B^n$ with $h_w(z) = z$, so that
\[
t_1(z) + (I + \Delta) t_2(z) = z+\Delta{t_2(z)} = z+w-h_w(z) = w.
\]
nodes.statement_short: Brouwer gives a fixed point, solving the equation for $w$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: A^n in the image
nodes.statement:
Therefore, all of $A^n$ is in the image of the map
$z \mapsto t_1(z) + (I + \Delta) t_2(z)$,
so that in particular
\[
A^n \subseteq \{ t_1 + g_1^{-1} g_2 t_2 \ : \ t_1, t_2 \in T \}.
\]
nodes.statement_short: Hence $A^n$ lies in the image.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Transport by g_1
nodes.statement:
Applying Lemma \ref{lem:nbhd_stability} with $\delta=\frac13$,
there is an $\varepsilon>0$
depending only on $K$ such that
$\{ g_1 t_1 + g_2 t_2 \ : \ t_1, t_2 \in T \}$ 
contains an $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of some point in $\mathbb{C}^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.2 transports the neighborhood by $g_1$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Extend to m terms
nodes.statement:
We conclude the same of the set
$\{ g_1 t_1 + \ldots + g_m t_m \ : \ t_1, \ldots, t_m \in T \}$
by choosing arbitrary fixed $t_3, \ldots, t_m \in T$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix the remaining $t_i$ to conclude for all $m\ge m_1$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Step (2): fattening
nodes.statement:
Proceeding to step \eqref{it_big_neigh}, let $k_1$ be a large integer
to be determined later, set $m_2 = m_1 k_1$, and for any $m \geq m_2$ write
$m = k m_1 + l$ 
with $k\ge k_1$ and
$0 \leq l < m_1$.

For each $j$ with $0\leq j<k$, applying step \eqref{it_small_neigh}
to $(g_{jm_1+1},\ldots,g_{jm_1+m_1})$, we obtain an $\varepsilon$-neighborhood
centered at some $v_j\in \mathbb{C}^n$. Further, we put
$v_k = g_{km_1 + 1} \overrightarrow{1} + \ldots
+ g_{k m_1 + l} \overrightarrow{1}$, where
$\overrightarrow{1} = (1, \ldots, 1) \in T$.
Since $m_1$ is fixed and $K$ is compact, 
we have $|v_j| \leq C$ for $0\leq j\leq k$, for some $C$ independent of the individual $g_i$.

Let
$N_\varepsilon=\{(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in\mathbb{C}^n:|z_1|^2+\ldots+|z_n|^2<\varepsilon^2\}$
be the $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of the origin in $\mathbb{C}^n$. Then by the
above observations, for any $\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_k\in[0,1]$,
$\big\{ \sum_{i = 1}^m g_i t_i \, : \, t_1,\ldots,t_m \in T \big\}$
contains the set
$$
\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e( \theta_j)(v_j+N_{\varepsilon})+e(\theta_k)v_k
=\sum_{j=0}^ke(\theta_j)v_j+kN_{\varepsilon}.
$$
By Lemma~\ref{lem:sq_root_avg}, there is a choice of
$\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_k$ for which
$\bigl|\sum_{j=0}^ke(\theta_j)v_j\bigr|\le C\sqrt{k+1}$.
Now let $k_1$ be the smallest positive integer satisfying
$k_1\varepsilon > C \sqrt{k_1 + 1} + 2$. Then for $k\ge k_1$, we have
shown that $\{ \sum_{i = 1}^m g_i t_i : t_1,\ldots,t_m\in T \}$
contains the closed ball of radius $2$.
nodes.statement_short: Fatten to contain the closed ball of radius 2.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Block decomposition
nodes.statement:
Proceeding to step \eqref{it_big_neigh}, let $k_1$ be a large integer
to be determined later, set $m_2 = m_1 k_1$, and for any $m \geq m_2$ write
$m = k m_1 + l$ 
with $k\ge k_1$ and
$0 \leq l < m_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Split $m=km_1+l$ into blocks.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Neighborhoods per block
nodes.statement:
For each $j$ with $0\leq j<k$, applying step \eqref{it_small_neigh}
to $(g_{jm_1+1},\ldots,g_{jm_1+m_1})$, we obtain an $\varepsilon$-neighborhood
centered at some $v_j\in \mathbb{C}^n$. Further, we put
$v_k = g_{km_1 + 1} \overrightarrow{1} + \ldots
+ g_{k m_1 + l} \overrightarrow{1}$, where
$\overrightarrow{1} = (1, \ldots, 1) \in T$.
Since $m_1$ is fixed and $K$ is compact, 
we have $|v_j| \leq C$ for $0\leq j\leq k$, for some $C$ independent of the individual $g_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply step (1) to each block, get centers $v_j$ bounded by $C$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Rotated sum of neighborhoods
nodes.statement:
Let
$N_\varepsilon=\{(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in\mathbb{C}^n:|z_1|^2+\ldots+|z_n|^2<\varepsilon^2\}$
be the $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of the origin in $\mathbb{C}^n$. Then by the
above observations, for any $\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_k\in[0,1]$,
$\big\{ \sum_{i = 1}^m g_i t_i \, : \, t_1,\ldots,t_m \in T \big\}$
contains the set
$$
\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e( \theta_j)(v_j+N_{\varepsilon})+e(\theta_k)v_k
=\sum_{j=0}^ke(\theta_j)v_j+kN_{\varepsilon}.
$$
nodes.statement_short: The image contains $\sum e(\theta_j)v_j+kN_\varepsilon$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2.3
nodes.statement:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:sq_root_avg}, there is a choice of
$\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_k$ for which
$\bigl|\sum_{j=0}^ke(\theta_j)v_j\bigr|\le C\sqrt{k+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose phases so the center has size $\le C\sqrt{k+1}$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Choose k_1
nodes.statement:
Now let $k_1$ be the smallest positive integer satisfying
$k_1\varepsilon > C \sqrt{k_1 + 1} + 2$. Then for $k\ge k_1$, we have
shown that $\{ \sum_{i = 1}^m g_i t_i : t_1,\ldots,t_m\in T \}$
contains the closed ball of radius $2$.
nodes.statement_short: Choosing $k_1$ large gives the radius-2 ball.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Step (3): continuous parametrization
nodes.statement:
Proceeding to step \eqref{it_cont}, we put $m_0=3nm_2$. Suppose that 
$m\geq m_0$ and $(g_1,\dots,g_m)$ are given, and choose a partition
of $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ into $3n$
sets $I_{j,\ell}$ (for $1\leq j\leq n$, $1\leq \ell\leq3$),
each of size at least $m_2$.
For each $j$ with $1\leq j\leq n$, write
\[
v_j = v_{j,1} = v_{j,2} = v_{j,3} = (0,\ldots,0,2,0,\ldots,0),
\]
where the $2$ is in the $j$th position. For each $j$ and $\ell$ we use
step \eqref{it_big_neigh} to express $v_{j,\ell}$ in the form
\begin{equation} v_{j,\ell} = \sum_{i\in I_{j,\ell}}g_i t_i
\end{equation}
for some $t_i\in T$.

Next, note that the set
$\bigl\{2[(1,\ldots,1)+\alpha+\beta]\ : \alpha,\beta\in T\}$
contains $D$. As in the proof of step \eqref{it_small_neigh},
we can choose continuous functions
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n), \beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n):D\to T$
such that
$z_j=2[1+\alpha_j(z)+\beta_j(z)]$ for every $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in D$.
Thus,
$$
z=\sum_{j=1}^n[1+\alpha_j(z)+\beta_j(z)]v_j
=\sum_{j=1}^n [v_{j,1}+\alpha_j(z)v_{j,2}+\beta_j(z)v_{j,3}].
$$
Finally, we use \eqref{eqn:step3_idecomp} to rewrite this as
$$
z=\sum_{j=1}^n\left[
\sum_{i\in I_{j,1}}g_it_i 
+\sum_{i\in I_{j,2}}g_i\big(t_i\alpha_j(z)\big)
+\sum_{i\in I_{j,3}}g_i\big(t_i\beta_j(z)\big)\right],
$$
which is a decomposition of the type required.
nodes.statement_short: Build a continuous parametrization of $D$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Partition indices
nodes.statement:
Proceeding to step \eqref{it_cont}, we put $m_0=3nm_2$. Suppose that 
$m\geq m_0$ and $(g_1,\dots,g_m)$ are given, and choose a partition
of $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ into $3n$
sets $I_{j,\ell}$ (for $1\leq j\leq n$, $1\leq \ell\leq3$),
each of size at least $m_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Partition indices into $3n$ blocks of size $\ge m_2$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Target vectors
nodes.statement:
For each $j$ with $1\leq j\leq n$, write
\[
v_j = v_{j,1} = v_{j,2} = v_{j,3} = (0,\ldots,0,2,0,\ldots,0),
\]
where the $2$ is in the $j$th position.
nodes.statement_short: Let $v_j=2e_j$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Represent targets via step (2)
nodes.statement:
For each $j$ and $\ell$ we use
step \eqref{it_big_neigh} to express $v_{j,\ell}$ in the form
\begin{equation} v_{j,\ell} = \sum_{i\in I_{j,\ell}}g_i t_i
\end{equation}
for some $t_i\in T$.
nodes.statement_short: Use step (2) to write each $v_{j,\ell}$ as $\sum g_it_i$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Continuous coordinate splitting
nodes.statement:
Next, note that the set
$\bigl\{2[(1,\ldots,1)+\alpha+\beta]\ : \alpha,\beta\in T\}$
contains $D$. As in the proof of step \eqref{it_small_neigh},
we can choose continuous functions
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n), \beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n):D\to T$
such that
$z_j=2[1+\alpha_j(z)+\beta_j(z)]$ for every $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in D$.
Thus,
$$
z=\sum_{j=1}^n[1+\alpha_j(z)+\beta_j(z)]v_j
=\sum_{j=1}^n [v_{j,1}+\alpha_j(z)v_{j,2}+\beta_j(z)v_{j,3}].
$$
nodes.statement_short: Write $z=\sum[1+\alpha_j(z)+\beta_j(z)]v_j$ with continuous $\alpha,\beta$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement:
Finally, we use \eqref{eqn:step3_idecomp} to rewrite this as
$$
z=\sum_{j=1}^n\left[
\sum_{i\in I_{j,1}}g_it_i 
+\sum_{i\in I_{j,2}}g_i\big(t_i\alpha_j(z)\big)
+\sum_{i\in I_{j,3}}g_i\big(t_i\beta_j(z)\big)\right],
$$
which is a decomposition of the type required.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute (3.1) to obtain the required decomposition.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Partition by residue classes
nodes.statement:
Let $q$ be the smallest prime number satisfying $q\equiv1\pmod{mn}$ and
$q\nmid\prod_{j=1}^n\mathrm{cond}(\pi_j)$. We put $t=\frac{q-1}{mn}$ and
define $S_{ik}^\circ(y)$ to be the union of residue classes
$$
S_{ik}^\circ(y)=\bigcup_{\ell=1}^t
\bigl\{p\in S(y):p\equiv tn(i-1)+t(k-1)+\ell\pmod{q}\bigr\},
$$
and
$$
S_{ik}(y)=\begin{cases}
S_{ik}^\circ(y)\cup\{q\}&\text{if }
i=k=1\text{ and }y<q,\\
S_{ik}^\circ(y)&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
Then the $S_{ik}(y)$ are pairwise disjoint and cover $S(y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Partition primes $p>y$ by residue classes mod a prime $q\equiv1\pmod{mn}$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Induction setup
nodes.statement:
For a fixed choice of $i$, let $v_k$ denote the $k$th column of $g_i$,
as defined in \eqref{eqn:gidef}, with the $\epsilon_p$ yet to be chosen.
We will show by induction that there is a choice of the $\epsilon_p$ such that
\begin{equation} |v_\ell - \mathrm{proj}_{\mathrm{span}\{v_1, \ldots, v_{\ell - 1}\}} v_\ell| \geq
\frac{1}{2r}
\end{equation}
holds for every $\ell=1,\ldots,n$, where $r=\sqrt{r_1^2+\ldots+r_n^2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Columns $v_k$ of $g_i$; plan to prove (3.3) by induction on $\ell$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement:
To that end,
let $k$ be given, and assume that \eqref{eqn:projspan} has been
established for $\ell=1,\ldots,k-1$.  Choose a unit vector
$u = (u_1, \ldots, u_n)$ orthogonal to $v_1, \ldots, v_{k - 1}$.
By the Schwarz inequality and the Ramanujan bound
$|\lambda_j(p)|\le r_j$, for each prime $p$ we have
$
|\bar{u}_1 \lambda_1(p) + \ldots + \bar{u}_n \lambda_n(p)| \leq
r.
$
Therefore
\begin{align} \frac{mn}{s(y, \sigma)}
\sum_{p\in S_{ik}(y)}
\frac{|\bar{u}_1\lambda_1(p)+\ldots+\bar{u}_n\lambda_n(p)|}{p^\sigma}
&\geq\frac{mn}{r s(y, \sigma)} \sum_{p\in S_{ik}^\circ(y)}
\frac{|\bar{u}_1\lambda_1(p)+\ldots+\bar{u}_n\lambda_n(p)|^2}{p^\sigma}\\
&=\frac{1+O_{m, n}(\sigma-1)}{r}, \nonumber
\end{align}
the latter equality following by Lemma \ref{lem:sump}.
We choose $\delta$ so that the $O$ term
above is bounded in modulus by $\frac12$, and
for each $p \in S_{ik}(y)$ we choose $\epsilon_p$ such that
$\epsilon_p (\bar{u}_1 \lambda_1(p) + \ldots + \bar{u}_n \lambda_n(p))$
is real and nonnegative. Then 
the left side of \eqref{eqn:inn_prod} equals
\[
\langle u, v_k \rangle = 
\langle u, v_k - \mathrm{proj}_{\mathrm{span}\{v_1, \ldots, v_{k - 1}\}} v_k \rangle \leq
|v_k - \mathrm{proj}_{\mathrm{span}\{v_1, \ldots, v_{k - 1}\}} v_k|,
\]
so that \eqref{eqn:projspan} follows for $\ell=k$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose phases aligned with a unit vector orthogonal to earlier columns.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Orthogonal unit vector
nodes.statement:
To that end,
let $k$ be given, and assume that \eqref{eqn:projspan} has been
established for $\ell=1,\ldots,k-1$.  Choose a unit vector
$u = (u_1, \ldots, u_n)$ orthogonal to $v_1, \ldots, v_{k - 1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $u$ orthogonal to $v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1}$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Lower bound via Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement_short: Ramanujan bound plus Lemma 2.1 give the lower bound (3.4).
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Choose delta and phases
nodes.statement:
We choose $\delta$ so that the $O$ term
above is bounded in modulus by $\frac12$, and
for each $p \in S_{ik}(y)$ we choose $\epsilon_p$ such that
$\epsilon_p (\bar{u}_1 \lambda_1(p) + \ldots + \bar{u}_n \lambda_n(p))$
is real and nonnegative.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\delta$ and $\epsilon_p$ making each term nonnegative.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Conclude induction step
nodes.statement:
Then 
the left side of \eqref{eqn:inn_prod} equals
\[
\langle u, v_k \rangle = 
\langle u, v_k - \mathrm{proj}_{\mathrm{span}\{v_1, \ldots, v_{k - 1}\}} v_k \rangle \leq
|v_k - \mathrm{proj}_{\mathrm{span}\{v_1, \ldots, v_{k - 1}\}} v_k|,
\]
so that \eqref{eqn:projspan} follows for $\ell=k$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify the left side with $\langle u,v_k\rangle$ to get (3.3).
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Determinant bound
nodes.statement:
Applying Gram--Schmidt orthogonalization to $v_1,\ldots,v_n$, it follows
from \eqref{eqn:projspan} that
$|\det{g_i}|\ge (2r)^{-n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Gram-Schmidt gives $|\det g_i|\ge(2r)^{-n}$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Norm bound and K
nodes.statement:
Moreover, by the Schwarz inequality
and Lemma \ref{lem:sump} again, each entry of $g_i$ is bounded above by
$1+O_{m, n}(\sigma-1)$,
so that $\|g_i\|\le2n$ for a suitable choice of $\delta$. Thus,
\begin{equation} K=\{g\in\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C}):\|g\|\le 2n, |\det{g}|\ge(2r)^{-n}\}
\end{equation}
has the desired properties.
nodes.statement_short: Entries are bounded so $\|g_i\|\le2n$; define $K$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Apply Propositions 3.3 and 3.2
nodes.statement:
We use Propositions \ref{prop:sw1} and \ref{prop:td} to 
determine a compact set $K\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$, a positive integer
$m_0$, and a real number $\delta>0$ with the properties described
there. 
Taking $m=m_0$,
the aforementioned propositions yield, for any
$\sigma\in(1,1+\delta]$, an $m$-tuple of matrices
$(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\in K^m$, elements $\epsilon_p \in S^1$ for each prime $p > y$, and
continuous functions $f_1,\dots,f_m:D\rightarrow T$
such that
\begin{equation} \sum_{i=1}^m g_i f_i(z) = z\quad\text{for all }z\in D.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Obtain $g_i\in K$, phases $\epsilon_p$ and continuous $f_i$ with $\sum g_if_i(z)=z$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Define t_p
nodes.statement:
Now, let $\mu=\frac{s(y,\sigma)}{mn}$.
For each prime $p>y$, we define
a continuous function $t_p : \mu D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ satisfying
\begin{equation} p^{- i t_p(z)} = \epsilon_p f_i(\mu^{-1}z)_k,
\end{equation}
where $(i,k)$ is the unique pair of indices for which $p\in S_{ik}(y)$ and
$f_i(\mu^{-1}z)_k$ denotes the $k$th component of
$f_i(\mu^{-1}z)$.
(Note that the lift from $S^1$ to $\mathbb{R}$ is
possible since $D$ is simply connected.)
nodes.statement_short: Lift to continuous $t_p$ with $p^{-it_p(z)}=\epsilon_pf_i(\mu^{-1}z)_k$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Error term
nodes.statement:
Define an error term $E(z)=(E_1(z),\ldots,E_n(z))$ by writing,
for each $j=1,\ldots,n$, 
$$
E_j(z)=\sum_{p>y}\left(\log L(\sigma+it_p(z),\pi_{j,p}) 
-\lambda_j(p)p^{-(\sigma+it_p(z))}\right).
$$
By the Ramanujan bound, we have
$$
\log L(s,\pi_{j,p})-\lambda_j(p)p^{-s}=O(p^{-2})
$$
uniformly for $\Re(s)\ge1$. Since $\sum_p p^{-2}$ converges,
the continuity of $E$ follows from that of the individual $t_p$.
Moreover, each component $E_j(z)$ is bounded by a number $C>0$, independent
of $j$, $z$, $y$, or $\sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: The error $E(z)$ is continuous and uniformly bounded by $C$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Choose eta
nodes.statement:
Set $R'=\sqrt{\pi^2+\log^2{R}}$.  We take $\eta\in(0,\delta]$
small enough that the condition $\sigma\in(1,1+\eta]$ ensures that
$\mu\ge C+R'$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\eta$ so that $\mu\ge C+R'$.
nodes.section: 3 Simultaneous representations of $n$-tuples of complex numbers

nodes.name: Linear part equals z
nodes.statement:
By \eqref{eqn:id_decomp}, \eqref{eqn:def_tp}, and
Proposition \ref{prop:sw1} we have
$$
\sum_{p>y}\lambda_j(p)p^{-(\sigma+it_p(z))}=
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{k=1}^n
\sum_{p\in S_{ik}(y)} 
\frac{\lambda_j(p)\epsilon_pf_i(\mu^{-1}z)_k}{p^{\sigma}}=z_j,
$$
for any $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in\mu{D}$.

nodes.name: Brouwer and exponentiate
nodes.statement:
Now fix $w\in R'D$ and define a function
$F_w:(C+R')D\to\mathbb{C}$ by $F_w(z)=w-E(z)$.
By the estimate for $E_j(z)$ above, the image of $F_w$ is contained
in $(C+R')D$. Thus,
by the Brouwer fixed point theorem, there exists $z\in(C+R')D$
with $F_w(z)=z$, so that
\[
\biggl(\sum_{p>y}\log L(\sigma+it_p(z),\pi_{j,p})\biggr)_{j=1,\ldots,n}
=z+E(z)=z+w-F_w(z)=w.
\]

nodes.name: Two-step plan
nodes.statement:
The proof will be carried out in two steps:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item
Applying our previous results, we
show that unless $P$ is a monomial (as described in Theorem \ref{thm:main}), 
for every $\sigma > 1$ sufficiently close to $1$
there are real numbers $t_p$ (for each prime $p$) and $t_0$ 
such that $P|_{s=\sigma+it_0}$
vanishes at $\bigl(\prod_pL(\sigma+it_p,\pi_{1,p}),\ldots,
\prod_pL(\sigma+it_p,\pi_{n,p})\bigr)$.
\item Simultaneously approximating the $p^{-it_p}$ by $p^{-it}$ for a
common value of $t$, we use Rouch\'e's theorem to find a zero of
$P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$ close to $\sigma+it$.
\end{enumerate}
Note that the second step is standard and is applied in \cite{SW}
in much the same way.
nodes.statement_short: Outline: zero of an Euler-product model, then Rouche via approximation.

nodes.name: Step (1): zero of the model
nodes.statement:
We begin with a polynomial $P$ whose coefficients are 
finite Dirichlet series $D(s)=\sum_{m=1}^M a_mm^{-s}$, and let
$y$ be the largest value of $M$ occurring in any of these coefficients.
We rewrite each $L(s,\pi_j)$ as
$L_{\leq{y}}(s,\pi_j)L_{>y}(s,\pi_j)$,
splitting each Euler product into products over primes $p\leq y$
and $p>y$ respectively. Setting
$$
Q(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
=P\bigl(L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_1)x_1,\ldots,L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_n)x_n\bigr),
$$
we have
$P(L(s,\pi_1),\dots,L(s,\pi_n))=Q(L_{>y}(s,\pi_1),\dots,L_{>y}(s,\pi_n))$.

The coefficients of $Q$ are rational functions of
the $p^{-s}$ for $p\le y$.  More precisely, for any monomial term
$D(s)x_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ in the expansion of $P$, the corresponding
term of $Q$ is 
\[D(s)L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_1)^{d_1}\cdots{}L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_n)^{d_n}
x_1^{d_1}\cdots{}x_n^{d_n}.
\]  Since the finite
Euler products $L_{\le{y}}(s,\pi_j)$ are non-vanishing holomorphic functions
on $\{s\in\mathbb{C}:\Re(s)\ge1\}$, the corresponding terms of $P$ and $Q$
have the same zeros there.

Let $D_1(s),\ldots,D_m(s)$ run through the coefficients of $P$ which do
not vanish identically, and consider their product
$f(s)=D_1(s)\cdots D_m(s)$. Then $f$ is itself a finite Dirichlet series
which does not vanish identically. By complex analysis, $f$ cannot
vanish at $1+it$ for every $t\in\mathbb{R}$, so there is some $t_0$
for which $D_1(1+it_0),\ldots,D_m(1+it_0)$ are all non-zero, and the same holds for the corresponding terms of $Q$.

Next we 
specialize the coefficients of $Q$ to a fixed value of $s$, obtaining
a polynomial $h_s\in\mathbb{C}[x_1,\dots,x_n]$. Considering $s=1+it_0$, Lemma \ref{lem:monomial}
implies that either $h_{1+it_0}=cx_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$
for some $c\in\mathbb{C}$
and $d_1,\ldots,d_n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$, or that there are $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb{C}$,
none zero, for which $h_{1+it_0}(y_1,\ldots,y_n)=0$.
In the former case, it follows from our choice of $t_0$ that
$P=D(s)x_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ is a monomial, as allowed in the
conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
Henceforth we assume that we are in the latter case,
and aim to show that $P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$
has a zero with $\Re(s)>1$.

We choose $R>1$ so that $R^{-{1/2}}\leq|y_j|\leq R^{1/2}$ for
every $j$.  By Lemma \ref{lem:poly_cont}, there is a number
$\varepsilon>0$ such that for every $\sigma\in(1,1+\varepsilon]$,
there exists $(z_1(\sigma),\ldots,z_n(\sigma))\in\mathbb{C}^n$
satisfying $h_{\sigma+it_0}(z_1(\sigma),\ldots,z_n(\sigma))=0$
and $R^{-1}\leq|z_j(\sigma)|\leq R$ for every $j$.  We use
Proposition \ref{prop:lem2} to determine $\eta$ in terms of
$y$ and $R$, and assume that $\eta \le \varepsilon$
by shrinking $\eta$ if necessary.
Proposition~\ref{prop:lem2} then guarantees that, for every
$\sigma\in(1,1+\eta]$, we can solve the
simultaneous system of equations
$$
\prod_{p>y}L(\sigma+it_p,\pi_{j,p})=z_j(\sigma),\quad j=1,\ldots,n,
$$
in the $t_p$ for $p>y$. For $p\le y$ we set $t_p=t_0$, thereby
completing step (1).
nodes.statement_short: Construct $t_0$ and $t_p$ so the polynomial vanishes at the twisted Euler products.

specialize the coefficients of $Q$ to a fixed value of $s$, obtaining

nodes.name: Perturb to sigma
nodes.statement:
We choose $R>1$ so that $R^{-{1/2}}\leq|y_j|\leq R^{1/2}$ for

nodes.name: Solve via Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement:
We use
Proposition \ref{prop:lem2} to determine $\eta$ in terms of

nodes.name: Step (2): Rouche
nodes.statement:
Turning to step (2), let $\sigma_1,\sigma_2\in\mathbb{R}$ with
$1<\sigma_1<\sigma_2\le1+\eta$, and put $\sigma=\frac{\sigma_1+\sigma_2}2$.
With the $t_0$ and $t_p$ resulting from step (1) for this choice of $\sigma$,
let $P_{it_0}$ denote the polynomial obtained from $P$ by replacing $s$
by $s+it_0$ in all of its coefficients, and define
\begin{equation} F(s)=P_{it_0}\!\left(
\prod_pL(s+it_p,\pi_{1,p}),\ldots,\prod_pL(s+it_p,\pi_{n,p})\right).
\end{equation}
Then $F$ is holomorphic for $|s-\sigma|<\sigma-1$ and satisfies
$F(\sigma)=0$ by construction. It follows that there
is a number $\rho\in(0,\frac{\sigma_2-\sigma_1}2]$ such that
$F(s)\neq0$ for all $s\in C_\rho=\{s\in\mathbb{C}:|s-\sigma|=\rho\}$.
Write $\gamma$ for the minimum of $|F(s)|$ on $C_\rho$.

Next, by abuse of notation, we write $P(s)$ as shorthand for
$P(L(s,\pi_1),\ldots,L(s,\pi_n))$. As
$P(s)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty a_mm^{-s}$ converges absolutely as a Dirichlet
series for $\Re(s) > 1$, there is an integer
$M > 0$ with
$\sum_{m=M}^{\infty}|a_m|m^{-\sigma_1}\le\frac{\gamma}3$.
By \eqref{eqn:Fdef} we have
$F(s)=\sum_{m=1}^\infty b_mm^{-s}$, where
$b_m=a_m\prod_{p|m}p^{-it_p\mathrm{ord}_p(m)}$, and
by the joint uniform distribution of $p^{it}$ for primes $p<M$, it
follows that the set of $t\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfying
\[\sum_{m=1}^{M-1}\frac{|a_mm^{-it}-b_m|}{m^{\sigma_1}}<\frac{\gamma}3\]
has positive lower density.  For any such $t$ the triangle
inequality yields $|P(s+it)-F(s)|<\gamma$ for all $s$ with
$\Re(s)\ge\sigma_1$, and in particular for all $s\in C_\rho$.
By Rouch\'e's theorem, it follows that $P(s+it)$
has a zero $s$ with $|s-\sigma|<\rho$.
Thus, $P(s)$ has zeros with real part in $[\sigma_1,\sigma_2]$, and indeed we have
$$
\#\{s\in\mathbb{C}:\Re(s)\in[\sigma_1,\sigma_2],
\Im(s)\in[-T,T], P(s)=0\}
\gg_{\sigma_1,\sigma_2}T
$$
for all $T\ge T_0(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate the shifts by a single $t$ and apply Rouche's theorem.

nodes.statement:

nodes.name: Apply Rouche and count
nodes.statement:
For any such $t$ the triangle
inequality yields $|P(s+it)-F(s)|<\gamma$ for all $s$ with

nodes.statement_short: Rouche's theorem yields zeros, $\gg T$ of them.
